part_title: RLHF — Learning from Human Preferences and Response Quality
review_basis: Original numbered AIF Module 03 WebP slides 38–40 visually inspected in sequence; image titles, examples, numbers and diagrams take priority over legacy lesson map.

scenes.title: What is RLHF?
scenes.narration: Reinforcement learning from human feedback, abbreviated R L H F, is a way to guide a model toward outputs that people judge to be more helpful, safe and appropriate. Read the numbered workflow from left to right. Step one contains a user prompt: how do I reset my password, reply in one sentence. Step two shows two candidate model answers. A says your password has been reset. B says use the password-reset link and follow the verification steps. This distinction matters. The assistant has not actually reset anything, so answer A makes an unsupported claim. Step three shows human reviewers preferring B. In step four, many preference comparisons train a reward or preference model to estimate which responses people are more likely to choose. Step five illustrates optimizing the original language model to produce answers more like those rewarded by this signal. Do not confuse the reward model with a live company policy database; it learns patterns of preferences, not necessarily up-to-date facts. The lower-left section explains why B is preferred: it gives a safe actionable instruction and avoids falsely claiming an action was performed. The warning at lower right is essential. Human preference alone does not guarantee factual accuracy. A response can sound confident and helpful while still being incorrect. For current or private company-specific reset procedures, the assistant may need a trusted retrieval system or authorized data source. Comprehension check: if a chatbot gives a polished but invented password-reset confirmation, should a reviewer reward it merely for sounding friendly? No. Honesty, actual task completion, and safety matter more than appearance.

scenes.title: RLHF: a chatbot feedback example
scenes.narration: This second picture reinforces the training loop with a different arrangement. The first panel asks the model to explain a password reset in one sentence. In the second panel, candidate A says contact support and follow verification steps. Candidate B falsely claims the password is already reset. Here the labels are intentionally reversed compared with the previous slide: A is the preferred response, not B. Always read the actual content rather than memorizing a letter. The third panel marks A preferred, because it gives the user a plausible next action without inventing a completed operation. Step four stores a comparison such as A preferred over B. Across many reviewed prompts, these comparisons can train a reward or preference model that estimates what humans consider better. Step five illustrates using that learned signal to optimize the language model, perhaps through a reinforcement-learning method. It is a simplified teaching workflow and real alignment systems may include additional methods and review processes. Below, the left panel says this can improve helpfulness and safety. The center identifies limitations: preference training does not inject live private policies into a model, and a human-liked answer can still be wrong or outdated. The right panel illustrates the solution for changing organizational facts: connect the system to a current, authorized retrieval or data source and check the retrieved answer. Imagine a university assistant that sounds very confident about the latest admission deadline. Even if its writing style is good, it should consult an authoritative current schedule instead of guessing. Which response in this slide is safer, A or B? A, because B asserts that an action occurred without evidence.

scenes.title: RLHF Process
scenes.narration: The heading says reinforcement learning from human feedback. Follow the four large numbered columns. First a pretrained language model receives a prompt, here explain cloud computing in simple terms, and produces candidate responses A, B and C. Pretrained means it has already learned general patterns from a large body of examples; we are not starting from an empty model. Second, people review the candidate answers and express preferences based on qualities such as clarity, accuracy and safety. In the illustration A gets a positive mark, while the other options are less preferred. Third, a separate reward model learns from many such comparisons. Its task is to predict how a human reviewer might rate an answer, not to independently verify every statement as true. Fourth, the language model is further optimized using the reward signal. The circular arrows on the right emphasize repeated training toward higher-rated responses. The lower-left example reminds us of the actual goal: a beginner asking about cloud computing should receive a clear and faithful explanation, not impressive technical jargon. The bottom middle decision cue is about model behavior and alignment, especially open-ended text responses where multiple answers may be possible. The takeaway reinforces that human preferences can guide a model toward more useful responses. However, high reward scores may reflect imperfections in feedback or the reward model, and alignment does not replace testing, moderation, or grounding in trustworthy sources. A final question: would training a reward model on a few thumbs-up examples automatically make a chatbot knowledgeable about this morning's company policies? No. Feedback training shapes response preferences, while accurate current facts require appropriate information sources.
